title: Why Do We Have Seasons? | Ask Huy
question: Why do we have seasons?
answer: Earth is tilted, and the tilt always points the same way in space. As Earth travels around the Sun, each half of Earth leans toward the Sun for part of the year and away from it for the other part. Leaning toward the Sun means a high Sun and long days, so it is summer. Leaning away means a low Sun and short days, so it is winter. That is why the north and the south always have opposite seasons.

visual.what: A cosy living room split in two. On the left Bối wears shorts and sandals under a bright sun. On the right she wears a big puffy coat in falling snow. Huy stands in the middle, Hùng holds a box of props, and Beo peeks out from a dinosaur coat.

parts.text: Bối, in summer you wear shorts and sandals. In winter you wear a big puffy coat. But why does the weather change at all?
Wait, it does not just happen by magic?
My winter coat is a dinosaur!

visual.what: Huy talks to camera, holding a calendar open on January. Beside him a small cartoon Earth sits close to a smiling Sun, and the top half of Earth is covered in snow.

parts.text: Here is a surprise. Earth comes closest to the Sun in early January. But January is winter in the top half of the world! Today we will find out what really makes summer, autumn, winter and spring.

visual.what: Bối points at a drawing of Earth moving close to the Sun, then far away. Beo holds up a crayon drawing of the Sun wearing sunglasses with a suitcase. Huy listens kindly, and Hùng warms his hands near a small heater.

parts.text: I know! In summer, Earth moves closer to the Sun. In winter, it moves far away.
Maybe the Sun goes on holiday in winter!
Two great guesses! The Sun never takes a holiday, Beo. It shines all year. And Bối, near a heater you feel warm, and far away you feel cooler. Lots of grown-ups think this too.

visual.what: Earth's path around the Sun drawn as a loop that looks almost like a perfect circle. A small label at the closest point says January, and the top of Earth there is snowy.

parts.text: But look at Earth's path around the Sun. It is almost a perfect circle, so the distance changes only a little. And Earth is closest in January, when the north is having winter!
Closest, and it is still cold?

visual.what: A world map on the same calendar day. Canada at the top is covered in snow with a snowman, while Australia at the bottom is sunny with a beach and a sandcastle.

parts.text: Here is another clue. On the very same day, it can be winter in Canada and summer in Australia. If distance made the seasons, the whole Earth would have summer at once.
Then what makes them?
The secret is a tilt!

visual.what: Hùng puts a lamp in the middle of a table as the Sun and carries a ball around it as Earth. A dotted loop on the table is labelled orbit, about 365 days.

parts.text: Step one. Earth travels around the Sun in a giant loop called an orbit. One full trip takes about 365 days. That is one year!
I brought a lamp for the Sun and a ball for Earth!

visual.what: A tiny Earth and a big Sun with a long arrow between them labelled about 150 million kilometres. Next to it, a short path from Bối's house to school, for fun.

parts.text: The Sun is about 150 million kilometres away. In one year, Earth travels about 940 million kilometres around it.
And I thought the walk to school was long!

visual.what: A globe with a straight line through it, labelled North Pole at the top, South Pole at the bottom, and axis along the line. Hùng spins the globe so fast it wobbles, with little dizzy stars around it.

parts.text: Earth also spins, like a spinning top. It turns around an invisible line that goes through the North Pole and the South Pole. That line is called the axis. One spin gives us one day and one night.
Oops! I spun it too fast. Now it is a dizzy Earth!

visual.what: Earth drawn with its axis leaning to one side, and a small angle mark labelled about 23 degrees between the axis and a straight up and down line. Bối leans back on her chair in the corner, copying it.

parts.text: Now here is the secret. Earth's axis is not straight up and down. It leans to one side, by about 23 degrees. We call that the tilt.
Earth is like me leaning back on my chair!
Maybe Earth is a bit sleepy.

visual.what: Four small Earths placed around the Sun on the orbit loop. Each one has an arrow showing its axis, and all four arrows lean in exactly the same direction.

parts.text: And the tilt always points the same way in space, all year long, wherever Earth is in its orbit.
So remember. Earth is tilted, and the tilt always points the same way.

visual.what: The Sun in the middle and Earth on one side of its orbit, labelled June. The top half of Earth leans toward the Sun and glows bright.

parts.text: Step two. Let's watch Earth travel. In June, the top half of Earth leans toward the Sun.

visual.what: Earth with a line across its middle. The top half is labelled Northern Hemisphere and the bottom half Southern Hemisphere. Beo holds up an orange cut in two halves.

parts.text: Each half of Earth has a name. Half of a ball is called a hemisphere. The top half is the Northern Hemisphere. The bottom half is the Southern Hemisphere.
Like two halves of my orange!

visual.what: The same orbit picture, now with Earth on the opposite side of the Sun, labelled December. The axis leans the same way as before, so the top half points away from the Sun.

parts.text: Six months later, in December, Earth is on the other side of the Sun. The tilt still points the same way. So now the north leans away from the Sun.

visual.what: Hùng holds the lamp still in the middle of a room. Bối walks around it holding a ball with a stick through it, always leaning the stick toward the window. Arrows show the top of the ball facing the lamp, then facing away.

parts.text: Your turn, Bối. I will hold the Sun very still.
Let me try! I walk around the lamp, and keep my ball leaning toward the window. Now the top leans toward the lamp. Now it leans away!
Exactly! For half the year, your half of Earth leans toward the Sun. For the other half, it leans away.

visual.what: Two playground pictures at lunchtime side by side. In summer the Sun is high and Bối has a short shadow. In winter the Sun is low and her shadow is very long.

parts.text: Step three. Why does leaning toward the Sun make it warm? First, the Sun climbs high in the sky. In winter, it stays low, even at lunchtime.
That is why my shadow is so long in winter!

visual.what: Hùng holds a torch pointing straight down at a sheet of paper on the table. It makes a small, bright, round spot.

parts.text: Torch ready! Oh wait, it works better when I switch it on.
A high Sun shines straight down. Watch this torch. Point it straight down, and you get a small, bright spot.

visual.what: Hùng tilts the torch, and the light on the paper becomes a big, pale oval. A small cartoon of butter spread thinly on a giant slice of toast floats beside it.

parts.text: Now tilt the torch, like a low winter Sun. The same light spreads over a much bigger patch, so each bit gets less.
It is like spreading a tiny bit of butter on a giant piece of toast!

visual.what: Two clock faces side by side. The summer clock has a long yellow daytime part and a short dark night part. The winter clock has a short yellow part and a long dark part.

parts.text: Second, when your half leans toward the Sun, the days are longer. The Sun rises early and sets late, so the ground has more hours to warm up. In winter, days are short and nights are long.
Short days? Does that mean early bedtime?

visual.what: A calendar strip with two big stars. One on 21 June is labelled longest day, summer solstice. One on 21 December is labelled shortest day, winter solstice. A tiny Sun stands still with its feet planted.

parts.text: The longest day of the year is called the summer solstice. In the north, it comes around 21 June. The shortest day, the winter solstice, comes around 21 December. Solstice comes from old Latin words meaning the sun stands still.

visual.what: The same calendar strip, now with two balance scales added, on 20 March and 23 September. Each scale holds a sun and a moon perfectly level, labelled equinox.

parts.text: In between, around 20 March and 23 September, day and night are about the same length. These days are called equinoxes, and they mark spring and autumn.
So spring and autumn are the in-between seasons!

visual.what: An outdoor swimming pool on an early summer day. Hùng dips one toe in and shivers, while a calendar on the fence shows an arrow from the longest day to about a month later, labelled hottest weeks.

parts.text: The hottest weeks usually come about a month after the longest day. The land and sea take time to warm up, just like a swimming pool stays chilly at the start of summer.
Brrr! Still chilly!
High Sun and long days make summer. Low Sun and short days make winter.

visual.what: Earth on its orbit with the north leaning away from the Sun. The top half is labelled winter with snowflakes, and the bottom half is labelled summer with little suns.

parts.text: Step four. Because Earth is tilted, the two hemispheres always have opposite seasons. When the north leans away and has winter, the south leans toward the Sun and has summer.

visual.what: Side by side in December. On the left, children build a snowman in the snow. On the right, children in Australia build a sandcastle on a sunny beach. Beo waves at both.

parts.text: So kids in Australia have summer in December?
Yes! In Australia, summer begins on 1 December. Some kids build sandcastles while others are building snowmen!
The snowman and the sandcastle can be friends!

visual.what: A world map with a band around the middle of the Earth. Northern Australia is highlighted, with a rain cloud on one side labelled rainy season and a dry sunny field on the other labelled dry season.

parts.text: Near the middle of the Earth, the temperature does not change very much. Many of these places have just two seasons, a rainy season and a dry season. The top part of Australia is like this.

visual.what: Two snowy polar pictures side by side. In one, a clock shows midnight while the Sun still shines over the ice. In the other, it is dark all day with stars and a clock showing noon.

parts.text: Near the poles, the tilt makes things extreme. In summer, the Sun stays up even at midnight. That is the midnight sun. In winter, some days have no sunshine at all. That is polar night.
Bedtime in daylight? I would need very thick curtains!
Then when does the Sun sleep?

visual.what: A farm shown in two halves. On the left a farmer plants seeds in spring. On the right a farmer gathers the crops in autumn, and Hùng carries a big basket of pumpkins.

parts.text: Seasons change how we live too. Farmers often plant crops in spring and harvest them in autumn.
And I carried the harvest all by myself!
So the season you get depends on where on Earth you live.

visual.what: Two Earths side by side. Our real Earth is tilted with four season pictures around it. An imaginary Earth stands perfectly straight, with the same plain weather picture all around it.

parts.text: Huy, what if Earth stood up straight, with no tilt at all?
Then the Sun's height and the length of the day would hardly change all year. Scientists think the seasons would almost disappear!
No more winter coat!

visual.what: Earth with a small tilt next to Uranus, a blue planet lying on its side with its axis almost flat, labelled about 98 degrees. Uranus has a little bandage and a sleepy face.

parts.text: Some planets lean much more than Earth. Uranus rolls around the Sun on its side, tilted about 98 degrees! Scientists think a giant crash long ago may have knocked it over.
Poor Uranus, it fell over and never got up!

visual.what: Hùng and Bối at a kitchen table with a grown-up nearby. Hùng shines a torch on paper while Bối traces around a small round spot, then around a big oval spot made by the tilted torch.

parts.text: You can check the torch trick at home with a grown-up. Shine a torch straight down on paper and draw around the bright spot. Then tilt the torch and draw again.
Hold still, Bối. Tilting now!
The tilted spot is bigger and dimmer, just like winter sunshine!

visual.what: Huy talks to camera beside a simple drawing of tilted Earth on its orbit. One side is labelled leaning toward, summer, and the other leaning away, winter.

parts.text: So, why do we have seasons? Earth is tilted. As it travels around the Sun, each half leans toward the Sun and then away. Leaning toward means a high Sun and long days, so summer. Leaning away means winter.

visual.what: A cartoon Earth whooshes along its orbit with speed lines, labelled about 30 kilometres every second. Beo hugs a chair leg and Bối holds on to the table.

parts.text: Fun fact. Earth zooms around the Sun at about 30 kilometres every second. That is fast enough to cross the whole width of the Earth in about 7 minutes!
And I cannot even feel it moving!
Hold on tight, everybody!

visual.what: Huy, Hùng, Bối and Beo wave under a bright blue sky with a big question mark. A friendly subscribe button with the words Ask Huy glows in the corner.

parts.text: Next time, we will ask why the sky is blue. Do not miss it!
Subscribe to Ask Huy and come back with your own questions!
Bye bye!

facts.claim: Earth is nearest the Sun in early January (perihelion around 3 January) and farthest around 4 July, so the Northern Hemisphere is coldest when Earth is nearest.
Earth's orbit is an ellipse very close to a circle (eccentricity about 0.0167), so the distance to the Sun changes only a little.
The northern and southern hemispheres always have opposite seasons.
One full orbit around the Sun takes about 365 days.
The Sun is about 150 million kilometres from Earth on average.
In one orbit Earth travels about 940 million kilometres.
Earth spins around an axis through the North and South Poles; one spin makes one day and night.
Earth's axis is tilted by about 23 degrees (23.44), and this tilt is the cause of the seasons.
Earth's axis keeps the same direction in space all year as Earth orbits the Sun.
For half the year the Northern Hemisphere leans toward the Sun, and for the other half the Southern Hemisphere does.
A hemisphere is half of the Earth; there are northern and southern hemispheres.
In summer the Sun is high in the sky and gives direct light; in winter it is low and gives indirect light.
Summer days are longer and winter days are shorter.
The summer solstice is the longest day and the winter solstice is the shortest; in the north they come around 21 June and 21 December.
The word solstice comes from Latin sol (sun) and sistere (to stand still).
Equinoxes come around 20 March and 23 September, when day and night are about the same length.
The warmest and coldest periods come about one month after the solstices, because the Earth takes time to heat up and cool down.
In Australia, summer begins on 1 December.
Tropical places, such as northern Australia, often have two seasons, a rainy season and a dry season, because the rain changes more than the temperature.
Near the poles there is midnight sun in summer and polar night with no daylight in winter.
Crops are often planted in spring and harvested in autumn.
Uranus is tilted about 98 degrees (97.75) and rotates on its side; the usual idea is that a large collision long ago caused it.
Earth moves around the Sun at about 30 kilometres per second, fast enough to cross its own width in about 7 minutes.

description: Why is it hot in summer and cold in winter? It is not because Earth gets closer to the Sun. Huy, his helper Hùng, Bối and little Beo use a lamp, a ball and a torch to show how Earth's tilt makes the seasons. This calm, science-checked video for kids aged 6 to 12 also covers solstices, equinoxes, opposite seasons in Australia and the midnight sun, plus an easy torch test you can try at home with a grown-up.

cast.role: the host (25): curious, warm, a little funny; explains

cast.name: Hùng
cast.role: Huy's younger brother (21), his hands-on assistant: sets up and runs the experiments and demos, brings things, now and then a funny little mishap

cast.name: Bối
cast.role: an 8-year-old girl who asks, guesses and tries things

cast.name: Beo
cast.role: Bối's 5-year-old little brother: curious, makes funny innocent guesses
